summary: This standards-track memo defines a standard set of hierarchical payment-related field names in XML, the Electronic Commerce Modeling Language, so that browsers can fill in forms for online purchases automatically. It is version 2 of the specification.

eli5.summary: When you buy online, you type your name and address again and again. This document defines standard names for those fields so software can fill them in.

questions: standard field names for online payment forms
subtitle: A standard set of names for the shipping, billing and payment fields that online shops ask for, so wallet software can fill them in.

tldr.problem: Every online shop used its own ad hoc fields and forms for addresses and payment details, which made manual entry tedious and error prone and made automated form filling hard.
tldr.mechanism: ECML version 2 defines a hierarchy of field names such as Ecom_ShipTo_Postal_City, with minimum entry sizes, plus an optional XML syntax (a DTD and a schema) to carry them. A Mode attribute marks each part as a query or an assertion.
tldr.outcome: Wallet and form-filling software from different vendors can ask for and supply the same fields. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3106, and it only names fields: protection of the data is left to other mechanisms.

today: RFC 4112 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2005 that updates RFC 3106, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says nothing about later adoption.

sections.title: Why Standard Field Names
sections.content:
Many parties do business on the Internet with ad hoc fields and forms, and the formats vary a lot from one to the next. Filling them in by hand is tedious and error prone. Software tools such as electronic wallets can store billing, shipping and payment information and use it to complete forms automatically, but the RFC says the spread of such tools was hampered by the lack of standards.

ECML (Electronic Commerce Modeling Language) provides a set of hierarchical, payment-oriented data structures so that wallets from multiple vendors can supply and query for data in a uniform way. Version 2.0 extends ECML versions 1.0 (RFC 2706) and 1.1 (RFC 3106), adding support for more payment mechanisms and transaction information and using XML as the example syntax. It is intended to meet the requirements of RFC 3505.

The RFC names two likely uses: consumer payment information input, which at that time still mostly happened through HTML forms, and business-to-business transactions, which more likely use XML documents.
sections.eli5: Every shop asks for your name and address in a different way. ECML makes them all use the same labels, like every school using the same names for the boxes on a form.

sections.title: The Field List
sections.content:
ECML v2 defines and names a hierarchically structured set of fields. The hierarchy is written into the names with underscores, so a request can target a whole aggregate such as Ecom_ShipTo (all the ship-to address parts a consumer is willing to give) or Ecom_Payment_Card_ExpDate (all the parts of a card expiry date). To conform, names and structure must follow the listed ones as closely as is practical for the syntax and protocol in use. Human-visible labels are not restricted.

The list is split by direction. Fields typically sent from the customer to the merchant cover three address blocks (ShipTo, BillTo and ReceiptTo), the payment card, loyalty card, order ID, user data, the schema version, wallet identity and the end-of-transaction flag. Fields typically sent from the merchant to the consumer cover the merchant and processor domains and the transaction identifier, URL, amount, currency, date, type and signature. A third group is for traffic between a merchant and a processor acting for it (usually a bank, called an acquirer), and many of those fields come from ISO 8583.

Each field has a MIN value: the minimum data size that MUST be allowed on data entry. It is not the minimum size of valid content. For example, a card number has a minimum of 19, the longest number the ISO standard allows, and a postal code has 14, believed to be the maximum required anywhere in the world.

Footnotes add rules. Street lines must be filled in order, so line 1 cannot be empty if line 2 or line 3 is used. Country codes use ISO 3166 two-letter codes. The ReceiptTo block is for when the party billed differs from the party receiving the receipt, for example with some corporate purchasing cards.
sections.eli5: The form boxes have names like a family tree: Ecom, then ShipTo, then Postal, then City. A helper can ask for one box or a whole branch at once.

sections.title: The XML Syntax and the Mode Attribute
sections.content:
The RFC gives an exemplar XML syntax as both a DTD and an XML Schema. If they conflict, the Schema prevails. The same names and structure may be used in non-XML syntaxes. The XML is deliberately liberal, because specific applications are expected to add their own constraints. For internationalization it relies on the general XML character-encoding rules, which mandate UTF-8 and UTF-16, and on the xml:lang attribute.

In XML the top element is Ecom, containing elements such as ShipTo, BillTo, ReceiptTo, Payment, Loyalty, User, Merchant, Transaction and TransactionComplete. Underscored names map to nested elements and attributes, so the ship-to city is a City element inside Postal inside ShipTo.

Every element may carry the optional Mode attribute with the value Query or Assert. It applies to all descendant elements until a lower element overrides it, so one attribute can mark a whole structure as a request or as supplied data. A query element may contain data, and that content SHOULD be treated as a default value to return if no better value is known.
sections.eli5: Each part can be marked as either a question ("what is your city?") or an answer ("my city is Oslo"). One mark on the outside can cover everything inside.

sections.title: How the Fields Are Used
sections.content:
ECML v2 only names fields and their hierarchy. It does not constrain the order or completeness of a request. A shop may ask for ship-to information first so shipping cost can be worked out before payment, or ask for everything at once. Version 2.0 cannot mark a queried field as mandatory, so all queried fields are optional to answer, although a party may still raise an error or ask again if something it needs is missing or looks wrong.

The communication method is open. The easiest for deployed software is fields in an HTML form, but an XML exchange, the IOTP Authenticate transaction (RFC 2801) or a proprietary protocol are also possible. On the web, the Ecom_SchemaVersion field is REQUIRED in every transaction so that browser software can tell which version it faces. It SHOULD appear on every page with Ecom fields and is RECOMMENDED as the last Ecom field on a page. At least one user-visible Ecom field is RECOMMENDED per page, because some software needs user activation.

The Ecom_TransactionComplete field marks the final page of a transaction, ideally just before Ecom_SchemaVersion. It stops automated fill from continuing to hand out personal data after the business is done.
sections.eli5: A hidden sign says which rule book the page uses, and another sign says "we are done now", so the helper stops giving out your details.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The information in many of these fields is sensitive. It should be protected from unauthorized modification and kept confidential when stored or sent over a channel where it could be seen, and its authenticity will often matter. The RFC does not specify the protection mechanisms. It suggests that, depending on circumstances, they might include object security (XML Signature, XML Encryption or CMS) or channel security (TLS or IPsec). Systems that store and later forward ECML fields will likely find object security most appropriate.

The user's control over release of the information is needed to protect privacy. Software on shared or public terminals should be configurable to fully disable memory of sensitive or identifying information, which is vital for library patrons, students, customers and children. Stored sensitive data should have an option to be protected, for example by a password. Multi-page fill mechanisms SHOULD check for Ecom_TransactionComplete and stop automated fill until further authorized. Hidden and default values sent to another party may be maliciously modified before they come back.
sections.eli5: Your name and card number are private. The helper should keep them locked away, never remember them on a shared computer, and stop when the shopping is finished.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to register the XML schema as urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:ECMLv2 and to create the urn:ietf:params:ecml namespace, where values are registered by RFC publication. The value v2.0 is registered permanently, so urn:ietf:params:ecml:v2.0 marks fields that conform to this specification. This is also the value of the Ecom_SchemaVersion field.

Three further registries are set up, each with additions by expert approval: Ecom_Payment_Card_Type (case-insensitive designations of one to four characters, starting from the 12 listed), Ecom_Payment_Card_Protocol (tokens, starting from seven including none) and Ecom_Transaction_Type (initially debit and credit).
sections.eli5: A public list keeps the official names and allowed words, so nobody invents two meanings for the same label.

sections.title: Changes from Version 1.1
sections.content: The appendix lists what changed from v1.1. The text was reworded to move the emphasis from HTML form fields to XML syntax. New items are the merchant-to-processor fields, Ecom_Wallet_Location and Ecom_User_Certificate_URL, the Mode attribute, Ecom_Payment_Card_IssueNumber, the loyalty card, device ID, valid-from and user data fields, an XML schema and an IANA Considerations section. There were also minor fixes related to telephone numbers and updated references for obsoleted RFCs.
sections.eli5: Version 2 added more boxes, a way to mark questions and answers, and a proper XML description.
